 First Horizon (FHN) Stock May Be A Bargain On Excess Returns

 Learn more First Horizon has delivered a near doubling for shareholders over the past three years, yet the stock has slipped recently, which puts fresh attention on whether the bank's current price is supported by the returns it earns on its capital. For investors watching a financial stock that has already moved a long way, the practical question is how much of its capital efficiency is already reflected in the US$21.76 share price. 
 The share price is up 97.6% over three years. This raises the stakes on whether First Horizon's capital returns are strong enough to underpin that kind of multi year gain. 
 The business model leans heavily on how effectively it can turn deposits and other funding into profitable lending and fee income. This can shape both the level and stability of the returns generated on each dollar of equity it employs. 
 Prefer to judge First Horizon on earnings? See what First Horizon's 15.0x P/E says about the price . 
 The stock's next move may depend on whether the returns First Horizon earns on its capital are high and durable enough to justify where the shares trade today. 
 If you want to explore the same question about the returns companies earn on their capital beyond First Horizon, scan through 40 high quality undervalued stocks . 
 Is First Horizon Still Cheap on Excess Returns? 
 The Excess Returns model looks at what First Horizon can earn above its equity cost and then links that to the share price. In this model, the bank is assigned a book value of $17.20 per share and a stable book value of $18.86 per share, while stable EPS is set at $2.39 per share based on estimates from 13 analysts. Against a cost of equity of $1.56 per share, the framework implies an excess return of $0.83 per share supported by an average return on equity of 12.68%. 
 Compared with a traded price of $21.76, that excess return stream is what the model uses to argue that First Horizon's estimated intrinsic value sits substantially above where the stock changes hands today. The gap reflects a setup in which the bank is expected to keep earning above its equity charge on a growing capital base, rather than relying on aggressive one off assumptions. For readers who want to see how that conclusion is built line by line, the full Excess Returns output is here. Find out what First Horizon could be worth using our Excess Returns estimate .
